1. Dataset Overview & Coverage Summary

This section establishes the scope and quality of the underlying dataset: total records, station coverage, fuel types represented, temporal span, and data quality flags.

Figure 1: Breakdown of 50,000 records by fuel type across 7,373 unique forecourts.

The dataset contains 50,000 price observations from 7,373 distinct UK forecourts, spanning 07 February 2026 to 16 April 2026. Data was sourced from the UK Government Fuel Finder API and aggregated by fuelcosts.co.uk. The dataset includes 6 fuel types: B10, B7_PREMIUM, B7_STANDARD, E10, E5, HVO.

The dominant fuels are B7_STANDARD (17,854 records, 35.7%) and E10 (15,082 records, 30.2%), together accounting for 65.9% of all observations. HVO and B10 are niche fuels with very limited representation (91 and 64 records respectively).

Data Quality Alert: 130 records (0.26%) contain price values outside the reasonable UK forecourt range of 100–250 pence per litre. These are likely data-entry errors (e.g., missing or misplaced decimal points, values in wrong units). Specific cases include:
  • B10: 9 below 100 p/L (examples: [10.31, 10.36, 14.31, 30.3]); 2 above 250 p/L (examples: [258.0, 921.0])
  • B7_PREMIUM: 9 below 100 p/L (examples: [1.0, 2.0, 21.9, 38.9, 50.5]); 6 above 250 p/L (examples: [265.9, 690.0, 799.9, 990.0, 1399.0])
  • B7_STANDARD: 26 below 100 p/L (examples: [1.0, 10.41, 19.9, 40.4, 41.4]); 10 above 250 p/L (examples: [1429.0, 1439.0, 1598.0, 1647.9, 1879.0])
  • E10: 23 below 100 p/L (examples: [1.0, 2.0, 10.1, 11.11, 12.1]); 16 above 250 p/L (examples: [999.9, 1000.0, 1239.0, 1299.0, 1359.0])
  • E5: 12 below 100 p/L (examples: [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 10.0, 10.21]); 15 above 250 p/L (examples: [1436.0, 1449.0, 1459.0, 1699.0, 1889.0])
  • HVO: 1 below 100 p/L (examples: [61.0]); 1 above 250 p/L (examples: [444.0])
All subsequent price analysis is performed on the clean subset of 49,870 records with prices in the 100–250 p/L range, unless otherwise stated. Raw (unfiltered) record counts are reported alongside for transparency.

Data completeness is 100.0% with 0 missing values and 0 duplicate rows detected.

6. Key Findings & Policy Implications

The following synthesised findings translate the data analysis into actionable insights for government policy analysts and energy economists working on consumer protection and fuel market regulation.

  1. Significant price dispersion exists within each fuel type Consumer Protection

    The max−min price range for B7_PREMIUM spans 144.4 p/L, and even within the IQR consumers face a spread of 30.0 p/L. For a 55-litre tank fill, choosing the cheapest versus the most expensive station saves up to £79.42. This level of dispersion — after excluding data-entry errors — indicates the market is not fully efficient and that improved real-time price transparency tools could yield material consumer savings.

  2. Update freshness is bimodal — many retailers are prompt, but a concerning minority have severely stale data Compliance

    The median update lag is 0.0 hours, indicating that many retailers update promptly. However, 1,802 records (3.6%) from 1,377 stations exceed a 7-day lag, with the worst case exceeding 53 days. This undermines the integrity of the open data scheme and limits its utility for real-time consumer price comparison. Introducing a maximum permissible reporting interval and automated non-compliance flagging should be considered.

  3. Fuel type coverage is uneven — premium and niche fuels have limited station reach Market Design

    Standard fuels (B7_STANDARD, E10) are available at the majority of stations, but premium (B10) and niche fuels are reported by far fewer forecourts. This limits price comparison for premium fuel consumers and weakens competitive pressure on premium-grade pricing. 796 stations (10.8%) report only a single fuel type — requiring complete per-station fuel-type reporting would improve the dataset's policy value.

  4. The fuel price hierarchy is consistent, but premium margins warrant scrutiny Consumer Protection

    The price ranking follows expected grade ordering: E10 (mean 145.2 p/L) is cheapest, followed by standard diesel, with premium grades commanding premiums of up to 42.2 p/L above standard unleaded. Whether these premiums are fully justified by production costs, or partly driven by weaker price competition in premium fuel markets, merits further investigation.

  5. Data quality issues from reporting errors erode analytical reliability Data Quality

    130 records (0.26%) contain implausible prices outside the 100–250 p/L range, including values near £0.01/L and above £18.00/L. These appear to be data-entry errors (decimal-point displacement, wrong units). The government fuel reporting scheme should implement automated validation rules (e.g., rejecting prices outside 100–250 p/L) at the point of data submission to improve data quality at source.

  6. Station coverage of the dataset is strong but uneven across fuel types Data Quality

    With 7,373 unique forecourts, the dataset captures the majority of the UK's approximately 8,000 filling stations. However, the variation in record density across fuel types — from 17,854 records for B7_STANDARD to just 64 for B10 — suggests that not all stations report all fuel types they actually sell. Mandating comprehensive fuel-type reporting per station would strengthen the dataset's value for monitoring market-wide pricing behaviour and detecting anti-competitive patterns.
